content: Blurred vision can occur in one eye (unilateral) or both eyes (bilateral). Historical Perspective There is limited information available regarding the historical context of blurred vision. Classification There is no universally accepted system for classifying blurred vision. Pathophysiology Blurred vision may arise from various causes, including refractive errors, opacities in ocular structures such as the lens, cornea, or vitreous, retinal disorders, or diseases affecting the optic nerve. Causes Blurred vision can result from a wide range of ocular and systemic conditions, including: Refractive errors (the most common cause) Age-related macular degeneration Cataracts Presbyopia Diabetic retinopathy Glaucoma Corneal abrasions or scarring; keratitis Conjunctivitis Uveitis Iritis Retinal detachment Retinitis Eye trauma (e.g., hyphema) Migraine Malignancies and tumors (e.g., brain tumors, lung cancer metastasis, leukemia) Optic neuritis Cerebrovascular disease (e.g., transient ischemic attack, stroke) Vasculitis (e.g., temporal arteritis, systemic lupus erythematosus) Hypertension Side effects of medications Epidemiology and Demographics Blurred vision can affect individuals across all age groups. Risk Factors Risk factors for developing blurred vision include: Genetic predisposition Family history of eye conditions Diabetes mellitus Advancing age Hyperlipidemia Hypertension Screening According to the American Diabetes Association, patients with type 1 diabetes should undergo a comprehensive eye examination within five years of diabetes onset, while those with type 2 diabetes should have an eye exam at the time of diagnosis. Annual follow-up exams are recommended thereafter. There is insufficient evidence to recommend routine glaucoma screening. However, the USPSTF advises individuals at increased risk, such as African Americans and older adults, to consult their primary care provider or eye specialist for guidance on glaucoma screening. The USPSTF recommends annual blood pressure screening for adults aged 40 years or older and for those at increased risk of hypertension. High-risk individuals include those with high-normal blood pressure (130–139/85–89 mmHg), overweight or obese individuals, and African Americans. Adults aged 18–39 years with normal blood pressure (<130/85 mmHg) and no other risk factors should be rescreened every 3–5 years. Natural History, Complications, and Prognosis The prognosis of blurred vision depends on the underlying cause. Diagnosis There are no established diagnostic criteria for blurred vision. A thorough history should be obtained, including the onset, duration, associated symptoms, and whether the blurred vision is unilateral or bilateral. History and Symptoms Common symptoms accompanying blurred vision include: Eye redness Eye pain Excessive tearing (epiphora) Headache Light sensitivity (photophobia) Halos around lights Nausea Excessive thirst (polydipsia) and urination (polyuria) Dizziness Numbness Physical Examination An eye examination for patients with blurred vision should include: Visual acuity testing Visual field examination Slit-lamp examination Ophthalmoscopy Tonometry Angle testing (gonioscopy) The presence of sudden hemiplegia, abnormal gait, ataxia, and dysarthria is indicative of a cerebrovascular accident. Laboratory Findings Patients with systemic disorders should undergo appropriate testing. Elevated blood sugar and HbA1c levels are seen in blurred vision caused by diabetes mellitus. Urinalysis and renal function tests should be considered in patients with hypertension. Antinuclear antibodies and elevated ESR are associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and vasculitis. A complete blood count (CBC) with differential and other tests may be necessary in cases of leukemia or multiple myeloma. Imaging A CT scan of the brain may help diagnose mass-occupying lesions or ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes. MRI of the brain and orbits can confirm optic nerve inflammation. Treatment Treatment depends on the underlying cause, and associated disorders should be addressed. Refractive errors and presbyopia can be managed with corrective lenses or eyeglasses. Supportive therapy for hyphema includes elevating the head of the bed, wearing an eye shield, and reducing physical activity. Wet macular degeneration may be treated with anti-VEGF medications or photodynamic therapy to inhibit the growth of new blood vessels. Laser treatment is an option for diabetic retinopathy. Pharmacologic therapy with eye drops is recommended for glaucoma. Infectious causes are treated with antibacterial, antiviral, or antiparasitic agents. Uveitis, iritis, and optic neuritis are managed with corticosteroids. Temporal arteritis is treated with high-dose corticosteroids. Hypertension is managed with antihypertensive medications. Surgery LASIK surgery is commonly used to correct refractive errors. Surgery is the primary treatment for cataracts and retinal detachment. Vitrectomy is used in the management of diabetic retinopathy. Glaucoma surgeries include trabeculoplasty, iridotomy, and trabeculectomy. Primary Prevention Preventive measures for diabetic retinopathy include maintaining a healthy lifestyle, controlling hypertension, stringent lipid control, and periodic ophthalmic examinations. Secondary Prevention Early detection and treatment of refractive errors in school vision programs are effective for preventing blurred vision due to refractive errors. Secondary prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease includes lifestyle interventions, weight management, antihypertensive agents, statin therapy, antiplatelet therapy, diabetes management, and smoking cessation.
